headline: Rain Cuts Narita Off From the Ground
deck: Record rain stripped capacity from Chiba’s roads and rails while Narita kept flying. The overnight passenger backlog cleared only when enough surface transport returned to move it.
body: Chiba station’s gauges recorded 351.0 mm on the calendar day, a 115.0-mm moving one-hour maximum and a 367.0-mm rolling 24-hour maximum; each was a record for that station [E2]. Those are three different accounting windows, and none is a prefecture-wide or national rainfall record [E2]. The distinction matters because the transport cascade was built on duration and timing as much as headline volume. By evening, the network was already surrendering alternatives faster than passengers could switch modes [E6][E8].

Rail disruption was public by 18:48 JST [E8]. NEXCO East logged the E82 closure at 19:01 and the E51 closure at 19:17 [E6]. JMA issued the revised Level-5 warning class at 19:30, telling people to secure their safety immediately; its use was a nationwide first for the revised class [E1]. The chronology places that warning inside a mobility system that had already begun losing redundancy [E1][E6][E8].

Narita kept operating on the air side. The transport ministry recorded no airport-facility damage that impeded operations, and flights continued [E5][E8]. The bottleneck moved outside the terminals: by 03:00, 6,680 people remained at the airport after high-capacity surface egress failed [E5]. An airport can keep its runway and still misplace the ground beneath its timetable [E5][E8].

That stranded population was a stock, not a permanent closure count. Travelers received water and sleeping bags overnight, with food also independently reported among terminal provisions [E7][E8]. By 09:00 the retained population had cleared after partial rail capacity returned, even while the wider transport network remained impaired [E5][E8]. The clearing rate identifies the overnight constraint: Narita lacked enough landside throughput to drain arrivals and waiting passengers [E5][E8].

Soga belongs in a separate ledger. About 4,000 people were estimated stranded around the station, while the SDF mission moved about 370 people [E3][E4]. The two numbers describe different populations and different jobs: one estimates the crowd around a transport node, the other counts people physically carried by the military [E3][E4]. Treating 370 as the stranded total would shrink the disruption; treating 4,000 as the SDF lift would inflate the response [E3][E4].

Chiba’s 17:00 prefectural snapshot listed five deaths [E3]. The five-death figure is a fixed-time casualty ledger and cannot serve as a final toll; evacuation orders, people using temporary facilities and those retained at Narita belong to separate accounts with different denominators [E1][E3][E5]. The same discipline applies to Level 5: it marks an emergency protective instruction, while roads, rail and airport retention followed their own operating clocks [E1][E5][E6][E8]. Combining those ledgers would turn synchronized stress into a single invented count.

By 14 August, Chiba Prefecture had opened management and finance consultations for affected small and midsize businesses [E9]. The notice created an advice channel; the supplied record establishes neither a new loan program nor a disbursement [E9]. A closure reading also fails the records: airport facilities had no damage impeding operations and flights continued while surface access broke down [E5][E8]. Narita’s effective passenger capacity, for one wet night, was set by the roads and rails outside the fence [E5][E6][E8].

art.caption: Chiba and Sakura set station records as roads and rail failed. Narita’s terminals kept operating while surface capacity disappeared.
